reader.summary: Egypt's dominant story this week was the government's push to secure parliamentary authorization for military support of Saudi Arabia against the Houthi threat. President Sisi declared Egypt ready to defend Saudi territory but ruled out an offensive strike on Yemen, framing the role as purely defensive. The parliament delayed its vote to October 26, keeping the decision in suspense. In a significant personal announcement, Sisi stated his presidency will end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the military to train future leaders. On the diplomatic front, Egypt formally rejected the Turkey-Libya maritime deal and opened talks with Greece to extend its eastern maritime boundary. Journalist Lina Attalah of Mada Masr was sent to trial after hours of questioning. Satellite imagery localized the gold mine at the Egypt-Sudan border reportedly hit by Egyptian strikes. The Egyptian pound fell to a record low amid regional tensions, while Banque du Caire moved forward with the country's largest IPO in a decade. A tourist bus crash killed 13 people. A husband appealed to the prime minister to intervene in his wife's detention.

display.eli5:
Here is what is happening in Egypt right now. President Sisi asked his parliament to give official permission to send military help to Saudi Arabia, because the Houthi rebels in Yemen keep firing drones at Saudi airports and ports. The parliament pushed the vote back to October 26, so next week the actual vote will happen. Think of it like a class voting on whether to lend their bike to a friend: the friend asked, the teacher said yes, but the class still has to raise its hands.

Meanwhile, a journalist named Lina Attalah who writes for an independent newspaper was questioned for hours by police and then sent to court. Next week, her trial is expected to actually start, meaning a judge will hear witnesses and she will get to tell her side. This matters because in Egypt, journalists who ask hard questions sometimes end up in court.

On the water, Egypt just told Libya, no, we do not accept your deal with Turkey about who owns the sea between you. At the same time, Egypt opened talks with Greece to push its own sea boundary further east. If those talks produce even a small agreement, it changes the map of the Eastern Mediterranean.

The big surprise would be if Egypt and Greece actually announce a framework deal in just one week of talks. That would be fast, and it would make Turkey and Libya very angry.
